etymologies.etymologyHTML: Alteration of earlier sailer, from Middle English sailer, sayler, saylere, equivalent to sail +‎ -or. Cognate with German Segler (“sailor”). Eclipsed non-native Middle English marinel, marynell (“sailor”) borrowed from Old French marinel (“sailor”). See mariner.

definitions.definition: In particular, a member of the crew of a (civilian or military) vessel, as opposed to a captain, admiral, etc.; a mariner; a common seaman.

quote.citation: 1873, Jules Verne, chapter I, in [anonymous], transl., Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Seas; […], James R. Osgood edition, Boston, Mass.: Geo[rge] M[urray] Smith & Co., →OCLC, part I, page 3:
quote.text: Merchants, common sailors, captains of vessels, skippers, […] naval officers of all countries, and the Governments of several states on the two continents, were deeply interested in the matter.

quote.citation: 2008, Cécile Corbel (lyrics and music), “Mary”, in Songbook vol. 2‎[1] (CD), performed by Cécile Corbel, Brittany: Keltia Musique:
quote.text: Mary is a sailordreaming of northern shoreslost galleons on the seaMary ever on her way

definitions.definition: A person who sails sailing boats (as opposed to boats powered by other means) as a sport or recreation.
A person who sails; one whose occupation is sailing or navigating ships or other waterborne craft.
Any of various nymphalid butterflies of the genera Neptis, Pseudoneptis and Phaedyma, having white markings on a dark base and commonly flying by gliding.
A stiff straw hat with a flat, circular brim and a low, flat crown.

quote.citation: 1909, Albert E. Edgar, How to Advertise a Retail Store, Including Mail Order Advertising and General Advertising: A Complete and Comprehensive Manual for Promoting Publicity, page 332:
quote.text: Straw Sailors. Children's large-leaf straw sailors, in new shapes, smooth or rough straw . Sizes 6 to 64. 80c, $1.00, $1.50 and $2.00. Milan sailors in new, large shapes, with white or cream ribbon.

quote.citation: 2023 October 20, Harry Inwards, Straw Hats: Their history and manufacture, Good Press:
quote.text: […] the trade that was done for some year in sailors for ladies.  […]  Developments of a fancifu nature in the brim formation in the direction of what is known as a "Breton" sailor, of which the characteristic is a slightly upturned edge, were the first to be made,  […]  But to-day, with the exception of straw sailors for girls and young ladies at school, there is very little demand for hats of this description.

definitions.definition: A brick, for example in a course of brickwork, that is laid vertically on its shortest end (smallest face), with its widest face facing the outside of the wall.
